name: Kira Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying pharmacy, so it's chemistry, how the body handles drugs and a lot of exams. I commute from my parents' house by bus, forty minutes each way, because it keeps costs down. After classes and on Sundays I work the till at my uncle's corner shop, which sells groceries and phone credit. My parents pay my fees and I cover my own travel and books. I pray five times a day, and I fit it between lectures, and I like my routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I thought. People get excited and then they find out machines are just machines. I'd tell my cousins to keep working hard and not to count on shortcuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm fine with it. I use the AI tool now and then to explain a drug interaction, but I check everything in the textbook. Nothing changing means the shop and my course carry on, which is good. But the shop's margins are thin already, and the supermarket across the road keeps taking customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. I'd keep the shop shifts, about 15 hours, and put 30 a week into savings for my own books and placements. I'd keep using the tool for explanations and not for essays. And I'd join the pharmacy society because they find placement spots for first-years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. I trust things to go on in their own time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cost on your list worries you most while you study, and what would you do if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop is what I worry about. My uncle says the supermarket nearly took a quarter of his sales last year. If he cut my hours, I'd lose about 40 a week, and I'd ask my parents for more, which I really don't like doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Think about the day you finish your degree. What do you picture yourself doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I see myself behind a counter in a hospital pharmacy, checking a prescription and explaining it carefully to an elderly man. I want to be trusted, the way our pharmacist was when I was little. It's a good job with respect, and I want that.

say: I'd say machines are just **machines** and tell my cousins to work hard.
think: Nothing changing is fine, but my uncle's **shop** is losing customers to the supermarket.
I use the AI tool for **explanations** and always check the textbook.
do: Keep the **shop** shifts at about 15 hours a week.
Save **30 a week** for books and placements.
Join the pharmacy **society** to find placements.
feel: **Settled**, trusting that things go on in their own time.
S0.quote: I want to be trusted, the way our pharmacist was when I was little.
fieldNote: Kira's calm comes from **routine** and faith.
She worries about her uncle's **shop** and her own hours.
She uses the tool with **caution** and checks the textbook.

steps.text: Keep working the till at my uncle's shop
Save 30 a week for books and placements
Join the pharmacy society for placement spots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful but not afraid. Some tasks will move to software, like checking and booking. I'd say pharmacists will still be needed for judgment, and I'd tell my cousins to see how it goes and learn what's proven to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit worried. A lot of what a pharmacist does is checking, and machines are good at that. Dispensing robots already exist in hospitals. I'd probably still have a job, but maybe with fewer colleagues. And my uncle's shop would have self-checkouts and ordering software, so it could go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools a bit more, once I see what hospitals actually use, not before. I'd practise checking what the tool tells me against the book. I'd also ask my pharmacy society about how hospitals are changing. And I'd talk to my uncle about whether the shop could add a service, like prescription pick-ups.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert but calm. I think change is fine when it's proven, and not when it's hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which jobs in your field, or the part-time work you do now, would AI touch first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop would go first. Self-checkouts and an ordering system are the first things the supermarket brought in. My uncle can only afford one of them. If he did, he'd drop the evening till, which is my shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change what you study, or how you study it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study the same but add a data and software element. I'd choose clinical modules where a person has to decide, because that's where machines are weakest. I'd stay with the pharmacist's role of checking and explaining. Patients want a person who looks them in the eye and explains the medicine.

I'd say pharmacists will still be needed for **judgment**.

My uncle's **shop** could go if self-checkouts and ordering software arrive.

Talk to my uncle about a **prescription pick-up** service.
feel: **Alert but calm**, because proven change is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast for families. I'd say we need to look after each other, and I'd say leaders should take responsibility and slow it down. I'd pray for patience, and I'd tell my family to stay together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared. If thinking work goes by 2028, even the checking in pharmacy could go and a hospital might not need as many pharmacists. My uncle's shop would be hit sooner, since people lose jobs and spend less. My parents depend on the family business network for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents and uncle about money. I'd get extra hours at the shop while I can. I'd ask my tutors what the hospital pharmacies are planning. And I'd think about switching to a clinical role in a community pharmacy or a nursing path, where a person is front and centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but I'd have faith. I'd feel the weight in my chest and I'd still go to class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family, and what would you do about your degree place and your loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut every cost, like phone data and new clothes. I'd ask my parents to be honest about what they can afford for my fees. I'd go to our imam and community for advice, because the community helps when systems don't. I'd also check what student support exists before I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, who or what would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean on my family and my community first. I'd lean on my tutors and the pharmacy society. I'd use the tools to learn faster, once I see they're reliable. I wouldn't count on companies or the government to look after us.

say: I'd say two years is **too fast** for families, and leaders should slow it down.
I'd tell my family to stay **together**.
think: Even the **checking** in pharmacy could go, so hospitals might need fewer pharmacists.
My uncle's **shop** would be hit sooner as people spend less.
do: Talk to my parents and uncle about **money**.
Take extra **shop** hours while I can.
Ask tutors what hospital **pharmacies** are planning.
feel: **Scared**, but with faith, and I'd still go to class.
S2.quote: The community helps when systems don't.
fieldNote: Kira turns to **family and faith** first.

She trusts tools only once they're proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare, so I'd tell my family to start. I'd say we should teach each other, and help those who struggle. And I'd say not to panic, because panic helps no one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be worried but with a plan. I'd graduate in 2029, and the AGI date is 2031, so I'd have two years in a job. Hands-on pharmacy tasks last till about 2034, but the checking could go sooner. I'd want to be the pharmacist who talks to patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, get placements in hospitals and community pharmacies, and save about 50 a week. I'd learn the tools properly and learn to check them. I'd also help my uncle try a service that supermarkets can't match, like a friendly prescription pick-up. And I'd help my parents put aside a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than with two years. It's not good news, but it's workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in those five years compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be trying to survive. With five years I'd finish and I'd be a working pharmacist with a few years of savings. That changes how I feel. I'd also have time to help my uncle and parents before it all lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At what point would you decide to stay on your course or change it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd decide at the end of second year. If hospitals are hiring pharmacists, I'd stay. If they're cutting them, I'd aim for community pharmacy or a clinical specialism, where a person is trusted to explain medicine.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to **prepare**, and we should teach each other.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 with two years in a **job** before AGI.
The **checking** part of pharmacy could go sooner than the hands-on part.
do: Get **placements** in hospitals and community pharmacies.
Help my uncle try a **pick-up** service.
feel: **Calmer** than with two years, and workable.
S3.quote: With five years I'd finish and I'd be a working pharmacist with a few years of savings.
fieldNote: The **warning time** turns Kira from survival to planning.
She sets her decision at the end of **second year**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so we should be sensible and not fearful. I'd tell my cousins to build a skill, a family and a faith. I'd say the world will change, but the basics won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel calm. I'd be 29, a pharmacist for six or seven years, maybe married with children. The robots arrive about 2039. I'd have a steady run. I'd worry a bit about my children's jobs, but that's far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work as a pharmacist, and save for a house. I'd learn the tools as they come, so I'm never behind. I'd stay close to family, help my uncle if I can, and give to charity. And I'd try to keep my faith steady through whatever changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a normal career and a normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having ten years let you do that two years wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years lets me build a family and a life. With two years I couldn't. It would let me look after my parents in their old age, which I consider my duty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who's thinking of starting your degree next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a friend to go for it, because people always need medicine and someone to explain it. I'd say learn the tools but check them. And I'd say keep family and community close, because they're what steadies you.

I'd tell my cousins to build a skill, a **family** and a faith.

I'd worry a bit about my **children's** jobs, but that is far away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because families and small shops wouldn't have time to adapt. What would help is honest information, community support, and the university helping us find placements and work in hospitals.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that my generation isn't careless. A lot of us are thinking about our parents, our faith and our families, not just ourselves.

headlineQuote: A lot of us are thinking about our parents, our faith and our families, not just ourselves.
portrait: Kira is a **pharmacy** first-year, 19, who lives at home and commutes by bus.
She works the till at her uncle's **corner shop**, and her parents pay her fees.
She is traditional and steady, uses AI tools now and then and always **checks** them.
Faith and **family** shape how she reads each scenario and what she would do.
Her mood runs from uneasy to anxious, and her uncle's **shop** is the weak point.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because families and small shops couldn't adapt in time.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **information**, community support and help finding hospital placements.
